schema.title: Credential
schema.description:
A login your users and systems connect with, over SFTP, FTPS, the web portal or the
S3-compatible endpoint. The API calls this resource `users`; the product calls them credentials.

A credential carries its own password, file access, permission and network rules, so each system
you integrate with can have its own, and revoking one leaves the others working.

Its file access takes one of two forms. With a **home directory**, `Permission` applies
everywhere the credential can reach, from `ChrootDirectory` down. With **virtual folders**
(`HomeDirectoryDetails`), the credential sees only the folders listed there, each with its own
permission, and `Permission` is absent.

Credentials created before a field existed may not have it, so treat everything not marked
required as optional.

Id.description:
Unique identifier for the credential. Generated by us and used in the URL of every
credential-scoped request. It is not the login name, although it is used as one when you do
not choose a `UserName`.

OrganizationId.description: The organization this credential belongs to.

UserName.description:
The name used to log in. Must be unique across the whole service, not just your
organization, so a name may be taken even though you have never used it. Check first with
the name-check endpoint.

Alias.description:
A label for humans, shown in the dashboard. Defaults to `UserName`. Setting it to an empty
string resets it to `UserName` rather than clearing it.

State.description:
Whether the credential can currently connect. `inactive` blocks sign-in while keeping
everything else intact. A credential also becomes `inactive` when it expires.

Permission.description:
What this credential may do with files, everywhere under its chroot directory. Absent when
the credential uses virtual folders, which carry a permission each.

- `none`: can connect, but sees nothing. The default.
- `read-only`: download and list.
- `write-only`: upload only; folders can be listed, files cannot be read. Useful as a drop box.
- `read-write-no-delete`: download and upload, including replacing an existing file, but
  never delete or rename.
- `read-write`: download, upload and delete.
- `full`: read-write, plus sharing files from the web portal.

Host.description: The hostname this credential connects to. Reflects your custom domain when you have one.

HomeDirectory.description:
The directory the credential lands in after connecting. Defaults to `/home/{UserName}`. Must
start with a forward slash and must not end with one.

ChrootDirectory.description:
The highest directory the credential can reach: it cannot navigate above this, so it never
sees other credentials' files. Defaults to `/`. Ignored while the credential uses virtual
folders.

HomeDirectoryDetails.description:
Virtual folders: the folders this credential sees, each mapped to a real location in your
storage with its own permission. Absent when the credential uses a home directory instead.

items.title: VirtualFolder
items.description:
One entry in a credential's virtual folders: a path the credential sees, mapped to a real
location in your storage, with its own permission.

Entry.description:
The path the credential sees, such as `/inbound`. Must start with a forward slash and must not
end with one, unless it is the root `/`, which must then be the only entry. Entries cannot
share a path or contain one another, and cannot contain a variable such as `${...}`.

Target.description:
The real location in your storage that the entry shows, as a path from the root of your
bucket. Must start with a forward slash and must not end with one. Two entries may show the
same location only if they give it the same permission.

Type.description:
Whether the entry is a folder or a single file. Defaults to `DIRECTORY`. A `FILE` entry
cannot be the root `/`.

Permission.description:
What the credential may do inside this entry. The same levels as a credential's `Permission`,
applied to this entry alone; `none` keeps the entry listed but denies everything in it.

SupportedProtocols.description:
How this credential can sign in. Normally `SFTP`, `FTPS` and `WEB_PORTAL`. A credential whose
virtual folders are too many or too deep to describe to the SFTP and FTPS service can sign in
only to the web portal, and lists `WEB_PORTAL` alone; shorten or remove folders to restore
the others. Absent on credentials created before this was tracked, which can use all three.

items.description: A way the credential can sign in.

Email.description:
Where web portal invitations and password resets are sent. Optional: a credential used only
by a machine does not need one.

EmailVerified.description:
Whether the address has been confirmed. Set when the recipient follows the link from the
email-verification endpoint; you cannot set it directly.

IsDefault.description:
Whether this is the organization's default credential, created with the organization itself.
The default credential cannot be deleted, and always uses a home directory.

SshPublicKeysCount.description: How many SSH public keys are attached, for key-based SFTP sign-in.

SshPublicKeys.description: The SSH public keys attached to the credential. Returned only when retrieving one credential.

items.title: SshPublicKey
items.description: A public key attached to a credential, for key-based SFTP sign-in.

UserId.description: The `Id` of the credential the key is attached to.

OrganizationId.description: The organization the key belongs to.

SshPublicKeyBody.description: The public key, in OpenSSH format.

Curve.description: The elliptic curve, for `ecdsa` and `ed25519` keys.

Comment.description: The comment at the end of the key, often the owner's name or machine.

Fingerprint.description: The key's SHA-256 fingerprint, as `ssh-keygen -l` shows it.

CreatedAt.description: When the key was attached, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

UpdatedAt.description: When the key last changed, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

Security.description: How the person using this credential proves who they are in the web portal.

MFA.description:
Multi-factor authentication for web portal sign-in. It does not apply to SFTP, FTPS or S3
connections, which authenticate with a password or key.

Required.description: Whether the person must enrol and use a second factor to sign in to the portal.

Factors.description: The second factors enrolled for this credential. Empty until one is added.

items.title: MfaFactor
items.description:
A second factor the person using this credential has enrolled for web portal sign-in. Factors
are enrolled by that person in the portal, not through this API.

Type.description:
The kind of factor: `totp` for an authenticator app, or `email` for a code sent to the
credential's email address.

Description.description: A label the person gave the factor when enrolling it.

CodeLength.description: How many digits the one-time codes for this factor have.

IsPrimary.description: Whether this factor is offered first at sign-in.

Protocols.description: Where the factor is asked for. Always the web portal.

items.description: A protocol the factor applies to.

LastAuthAt.description: When the factor was last used to sign in, in Unix epoch milliseconds, or `null`.

CreatedAt.description: When the factor was enrolled, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

UpdatedAt.description: When the factor last changed, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

Network.description: Where this credential may connect from, in addition to your organization's own rules.

InboundRules.description:
Rules that allow connections to this credential, on top of your organization's rules. See
the inbound rule object for how they combine. Empty by default.

items.title: InboundRule
items.description:
One network rule that allows connections to a credential from an address or range.

A connection is accepted when **any** enabled `allow` rule matches its protocol and source
address, counting your organization's rules and the credential's own together. So a credential's
rules can only add to what the organization already allows, never restrict it. New organizations
start with one organization rule that allows every address; tighten that rule before credential
rules make a difference.

Id.description:
An identifier for the rule, unique within the credential. You choose it; the dashboard uses a
UUID.

Protocol.description:
Which connections the rule applies to: `*` for every protocol, or one of `SFTP`, `FTPS` or
`WEB_PORTAL`. Values are case-sensitive.

State.description: Whether the rule is in effect. A `disabled` rule is kept but never matches.

Action.description:
What a matching connection is allowed to do. Only `allow` rules are evaluated, so `allow` is
the only value with an effect.

Source.description:
Where the connection comes from: a single IPv4 or IPv6 address, or a CIDR range such as
`203.0.113.0/24`.

Description.description: A note explaining why the rule exists. Shown in the dashboard.

ExpiresAt.description:
When access stops working, in **Unix epoch seconds**, or `null` or absent if it never expires.

Once that time passes (checked every few minutes) the credential becomes `inactive` and
`ExpiresAt` returns to `null`, so an expired credential reads like a deactivated one with no
expiry. Activating it again restores access with no expiry.

LastLogin.description:
The most recent sign-in, or `null` if the credential has never been used. Not returned when a
credential is first created.

oneOf.description: The credential has never been used.

oneOf.title: LastLogin
oneOf.description: The most recent time this credential connected, and from where.

Id.description: The identifier of the audit log event that recorded the login.

Timestamp.description: When the login happened, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

IpAddress.description:
The address the connection came from, anonymized: an IPv4 address keeps its first three
parts and an IPv6 address its first 48 bits, with the rest zeroed.

OriginalIpAddress.description: The full address the connection came from.

Geo.description:
Where that address is, approximately, or `null` when it could not be located. Location is
looked up from the address, so a connection through a VPN or proxy shows the proxy.

oneOf.description: The address could not be located.
The approximate location of the address.

UserAgent.description:
The connecting client as it identified itself, parsed into the client, its operating system
and its device, or `null` when it sent nothing. Parts that cannot be recognised are `Other`
or `null`.

oneOf.description: The client did not identify itself.

userAgent.description: The raw identification string the client sent.

patchMinor.description: The version part after the patch, when there is one.

LoginsCount.description: How many times this credential has signed in. Not returned when it is first created.

Password.description:
The current password, in plain text.

Unusually for an API, this is returned on every read: we hold passwords so that they can be
shown in the dashboard and rotated for you. Treat any response containing a credential as a
secret: do not log it, cache it, or send it to a browser you do not control.

PasswordCreatedAt.description:
When the current password was set, as an ISO 8601 timestamp. Use it to find credentials due
for rotation. Not returned when a credential is created.

URI.description:
A ready-to-use connection string combining the login name, password and host. Contains the
password in clear text, so it carries the same handling rules.

CreatedAt.description: When the credential was created, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

UpdatedAt.description: When the credential was last changed, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

default.summary: A credential that has been in use

400.description:
The request body failed validation. Nothing was changed.

`errors` says which fields were rejected and why, in one of two forms: an object keyed by field
name, or a list of fields. Handle both. This is a problem with the request: fix it rather than
retrying.

schema.title: Error
schema.description:
Every error response from the API uses this shape. Match on `id`, which is stable, rather than on
`message`, which is written for humans and may be reworded.

id.description:
A stable, machine-readable code for the error, such as `invalid_request_body`, `not_found`
or `internal_server_error`.

message.description: A human-readable explanation, safe to log but not intended for end users verbatim.

errors.description:
Which fields of the request were rejected and why. Present only on `400` responses, in one of
two forms: an object keyed by field name, from the checks every request goes through, or a
list of fields, from the checks that need your organization's own state, such as whether two
virtual folders overlap. Handle both.

oneOf.title: ValidationError
oneOf.description:
Field-level detail, present only on `400` responses caused by a malformed request body.

Each field the endpoint validates appears as its own property, keyed by the field name exactly as
it was sent; nested fields use dotted paths such as `Settings.Network`. Fields that passed are
listed too, carrying `isInvalid: false` and an empty message — so find the failures by filtering
on `isInvalid` rather than assuming only failures are present.

isValid.description: Always `false` when this object is returned.

additionalProperties.description: The outcome for one field of the request body.

message.description: Why the field was rejected. Empty when the field passed.

HasActions.message: You must include at least one action.

items.title: FieldError
items.description: One field that was rejected, and why.

field.description: The name of the field, as it was sent.

message.description: Why the field was rejected, written for a person.
examples: Unfortunately, two virtual folders can't share the same path.

fields.summary: A field failed the checks every request goes through

UserName.message: Unfortunately, username can't be shorter than 5 characters.

errors.message: Unfortunately, two virtual folders can't share the same path.

401.description:
The request was not authenticated.

Usually the `Authorization` header is missing or malformed, the key has been revoked, or the key
belongs to a different organization than the one in the path. It is also returned when the
organization is not in an active state.

Note the two body shapes. When authentication fails, the request never reaches a handler and the
gateway returns a bare `message`. When a handler rejects a request for its own reasons, you get
the standard error object with an `id`. Code defensively for both.

schema.title: UnauthorizedError
schema.description:
The body of a `401`. It has two sources, and they do not return quite the same thing.

When authentication itself fails, the request is rejected at the edge and never reaches the
endpoint, so the body carries only `message`. When an endpoint rejects an already-authenticated
request, you get the standard error object including `id`. Treat `id` as optional on this status
and on this status only.

id.description:
A stable, machine-readable code. Absent when the request was rejected before reaching the
endpoint.

message.description: A human-readable explanation of why the request was not authenticated.

403.description: The update would give the credential more than 250 inbound rules.

404.description:
No such credential, or it belongs to another organization.

The API does not distinguish between the two, so that a credential's existence in another
organization cannot be probed.

500.description:
Something failed on our side.

The request may or may not have taken effect, so read the credential back before retrying a
change. Retrying a read is always safe. If it persists, contact support with the approximate time
of the request.
